solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Alaskan city's branch or agency downsized

indicators.note: a downsized firm has been cut back, so the phrase loses letters from both ends and what remains is kept

parts.note: drop BR from the front and NCY from the back; the rest runs across the word break

explanation.surface: A news item about a firm cutting back its office in an Alaskan city.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s joins definition to wordplay: the city ‘has’ the phrase inside it. ‘Downsized’ reads as corporate cost-cutting, which suits branch and agency perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this port on Cook Inlet is the most populous city in the state.

clue.text: Religious leader and a bishop on program

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing placed on another sits above it

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
a bot is an automated computer program

explanation.surface: A church leader and a bishop appearing together on a broadcast programme.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Program’ with its American spelling points to software rather than television, which is the nudge towards BOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the head of a community of monks leads it in religious life.

clue.text: Sweet creature eats dairy periodically

indicators.note: what an animal eats ends up inside it, so the creature takes the letters in
something done periodically recurs at intervals, so take every other letter

explanation.surface: Some sugary animal nibbling dairy produce every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: The camel opens after its first letter to swallow the pair. ‘Sweet creature’ looks like a term of endearment, but the adjective is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the noun sense: a chewy sweet, or toffee, made from boiled sugar and butter.

clue.text: Bananas gone on ripe tree

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, and letters that have gone crazy end up in a new order

explanation.surface: Bananas left on a ripening tree until they go off.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Bananas’ looks like the fruit on the tree, but it is the anagram indicator; only ‘tree’ is definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is a regional name for the Douglas fir, a conifer of the American Northwest.

clue.text: Leader leaves more nuts for summer?

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter, and when it leaves the word loses its head

explanation.surface: A leader departs, leaving a greater stock of nuts for the summer months.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Summer’ is one who sums, not the season; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword-only sense: read summer as ‘one who sums’, and a person or device that adds numbers qualifies.

clue.text: Plant, say, on road plating metal

indicators.note: in a down clue, the first piece sits on top of what follows
plating is a metal coating wrapped round something, so the road wraps round the metal

explanation.surface: A plant, for example, beside a road with metal sheeting.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Plating metal’ sounds like electroplating, where the metal is the coating; here the road does the covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: it is the sweet briar, a wild rose with scented leaves.

clue.text: Some soldiers almost laugh involuntarily

indicators.note: almost the whole word means stopping one short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: actors’ slang for breaking into helpless laughter on stage

explanation.surface: A few soldiers who cannot help giggling.
explanation.walkthrough: Theatre slang turns a noun about the dead into a verb about fits of giggles, which is why the surface feels so harmless.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an army corps is a body of soldiers, usually two or more divisions.

clue.text: It can make parting company bearable at first

parts.note: the .com suffix marks a commercial company

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Something that makes leaving a firm easier to bear.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Parting company’ reads as a phrase about leaving, but the parting is the line in your hair and ‘company’ is split off as wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: drawing a comb through hair is how the dividing line called a parting is made.

clue.text: Period covered by cost of living? That should get a reaction

indicators.note: something covered by a thing sits under it, so the period goes inside the cost

parts.note: the payment for somewhere to live
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Grumbling about the cost of living, meant to provoke a response.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the pun: the ‘cost of living’ is literally what you pay to live in a place, not the economists’ index.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: chemists add this substance to a mixture precisely to produce a reaction.

clue.text: Grumpy companion follows friends the wrong way — reckless!

indicators.note: going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the word is read in reverse
a thing that follows comes after, so the companion goes second

parts.note: Grumpy and his fellow dwarf in Snow White

explanation.surface: A sulky partner trails along behind friends, heading the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Grumpy’ looks like an adjective, but capitalised it is one of Snow White’s seven dwarfs, and his companion is another dwarf.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word describes a cheerfully careless, devil-may-care attitude.

clue.text: Animated character with goal to serve drinks

indicators.note: one thing with another means the two go together side by side

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure whose aim is to pour drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Goal’ sounds like football but means an aim, as in ‘to what end?’.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb comes from the noun for someone who works behind a bar pouring drinks.

clue.text: Priest protecting poor moves out of Brazil

indicators.note: to protect something is to put yourself round it, so the priest wraps the other word

parts.note: a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist priest

explanation.surface: A cleric sheltering the poor who are being driven out of Brazil.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Moves out of Brazil’ reads like migration, but the moves are dance steps.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: this fast, close partner dance originated in Brazil and swept the world in 1989.

clue.text: Largely subdued spy drinks martini finally — it's shaken not stirred

definitions.note: the definition is a description: a tambourine is something shaken

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so keep most of the word and drop its last letter
what someone drinks goes inside them, so the spy takes the letter in
what comes finally is at the end, so take the last letter

explanation.surface: A secret agent orders his martini the James Bond way.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Shaken not stirred’ is Bond’s martini order, so Bond is the spy you reach for; the letters need Bourne, and the thing shaken is a percussion instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: this small frame drum with jingles is played by shaking it, and nobody stirs one.

clue.text: Unenthusiastic response crushes small network

indicators.note: to crush something is to squeeze it, here squeezed tight inside the response

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A lukewarm reaction squashes a small business network.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Network’ suggests computers or contacts; here it is simply a net.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a net of interlaced strands with open spaces is a network in the literal sense.

clue.text: Abruptly left desk, dazed and confused

indicators.note: something dazed has been knocked senseless, and the letters are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: Someone bolts from their desk in a daze.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Confused’ looks like a second anagram indicator, but it is a plain synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the informal verb means to run off in a hurry.

clue.text: Plant 41 stops work

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so the number is plugged inside the other word

explanation.surface: A plant closes down factory number 41.
explanation.walkthrough: A 15×15 grid has no 41, so this is not a cross-reference: the number is meant as Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a woodland flower related to the primrose and cowslip.

clue.text: Sort queen out if one asks for it

indicators.note: sorting something out rearranges it, so the letters go into a new order

explanation.surface: An offer to deal with the monarch’s problem if asked.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Sort’ looks like the anagram indicator, but it is fodder; ‘out’ does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: something available when asked for is offered in this phrase.

clue.text: Quest — pick outrageous dance

indicators.note: outrageous behaviour is wild and out of order, as the letters become

explanation.surface: A challenge to choose some shocking dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Q and K are the giveaway: few dances use both.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a lively ballroom dance in quick time.

clue.text: Coin toss for fantasy sport

parts.note: quid is British slang for a pound, and there is a pound coin

explanation.surface: Tossing a coin at the start of a match.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Coin toss’ reads as the ritual before kick-off; here ‘toss’ means throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the airborne ball game played on broomsticks in the Harry Potter books.

clue.text: Antique unit to get angry about state museum's leader

indicators.note: about means around, so the anger goes round the other letters

parts.note: to rile is to anger; be riled, get angry

indicators.note: the leader goes first, so take the opening letter

explanation.surface: An antique piece that angers the state museum’s director.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Antique unit’ suggests a piece of old furniture near a museum, but it is a unit of distance.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ancient measure of a thousand paces, about 1,480 metres, is a unit from antiquity.

clue.text: Part of US train disturbed calm air

indicators.note: disturbed things are thrown out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Turbulence ruffles the still air around an American train.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘US’ flags American usage: the British term would be carriage or van.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: Americans call a railway carriage a car, and this one carries the post.

clue.text: English city is a close match?

definitions.meaning: a city in the East Midlands
a game between teams from the same area

explanation.walkthrough: ‘Close’ means near in place, not tight on the scoreboard: a local derby is played between neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: an East Midlands city, and a match between local rivals who are close geographically.

clue.text: Kind of music paper publishing rubbish magazine

parts.note: a rag is a low-quality newspaper
Time is an American news magazine

explanation.surface: A music paper printing a trashy magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Paper publishing rubbish’ is one long definition of a single word, so don’t look for three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a syncopated piano style popular around 1900.

clue.text: Leave South American capital briefly

indicators.note: to put it briefly is to cut it short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: Quito is the capital of Ecuador

explanation.surface: A quick departure from a South American capital.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Leave’ could be a noun (holiday), but the answer is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to quit a place or job is to leave it.

clue.text: Artist's editor wise to pull back

indicators.note: pulling back means going backwards, so the pair of words is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A painter’s editor, shrewd enough to hold back.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Pull back’ looks like a phrase meaning retreat, but ‘back’ reverses both wise and pull together; ‘to’ just runs them on.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the French Impressionist famous for ballet dancers.

clue.text: Fancy cereal seen regularly in African city

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so take every second letter

parts.note: the even letters of fancy then cereal

explanation.surface: Posh breakfast food often found in an African city.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters run across the word break: A, C from fancy and C, R, A from cereal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the coastal capital of Ghana in West Africa.

clue.text: In speech, refers to locations

indicators.note: in speech means as spoken, so the word is taken by sound, not spelling

parts.note: to cite a source is to refer to it

explanation.surface: A speaker mentions some places.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are said the same; the spelling follows the definition, locations.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: places where something is or happens.

clue.text: Rising late, nearly curses

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means going upwards, so the letters are read from bottom to top
nearly the whole word means one letter short, so the last goes

explanation.surface: Someone who oversleeps and nearly swears about it.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Curses’ looks like a plural noun or verb, but read it as the exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: An interjection for an interjection: both are mild oaths of annoyance.

clue.text: Save king's boring quotation?

indicators.note: to bore is to drill a hole, so the king drills into the other word

parts.note: save = except, as in ‘all save one’

explanation.surface: Rescuing a monarch’s tedious remark.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Boring’ reads as dull but means drilling in; ‘Save’ reads as rescue but means except.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, marked with a question mark: a quotation is one kind of extract taken from a text.

clue.text: It's played by chamber musician

indicators.note: letters played with are moved about into a new order
by means beside, so the two pieces sit next to each other

parts.note: a cell is a small chamber

explanation.surface: A remark that the piece is performed by a chamber ensemble player.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Chamber musician’ looks like a single phrase, but ‘chamber’ is wordplay and ‘musician’ alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a player of the cello, often found in chamber groups.

clue.text: Card deck returned to snitch

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: A pack of cards sent back to an informer.
explanation.walkthrough: ‘Returned to’ reads as a phrase about sending back, but ‘to’ is a piece of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a deck of 78 cards used in fortune-telling.

clue.text: Man to deal with topping for loaf

parts.note: to address a problem is to deal with it

explanation.surface: A baker working out what to put on top of a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: Loaf is rhyming slang: loaf of bread = head. So a topping for the loaf is something worn on the head, not a glaze.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang: loaf means head, so the ornamental covering worn on it tops the loaf.
